Long ago, a child named Ember passed through the houses one evening. She carried a burning ember in a clay pot, and when she stopped at each home, she whispered the name of the fire: “Flame.” The people nodded, grateful for the warmth, but said nothing.

The next day, Ember returned. This time, she passed through again, and at each house, she repeated the name: “Flame.” But no one dared to speak it aloud.

On the third night, Ember came once more. As she passed, she called out the name, “Flame,” and this time, one person spoke it back: “Flame.” The sound was light, like wind through a hallway. But when she returned the next day and said it again, many voices answered—“Flame, flame, flame”—and the house trembled.

The elders said: “The name is strong. If we say it too many times, the fire will burn too bright, and the house will collapse.”

So they stopped. But Ember kept coming.

It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.
